entries.title: GOP state officials push to revive Trump's mail voting restrictions for 2028 election
entries.summary: Some Republican state officials are reviving a bid for mail-in voting restrictions for the 2028 election by appealing a court order blocking the Postal Service from carrying out a revised ballot rule.
entries.content:
GOP state officials push to revive Trump's mail voting restrictions for 2028 election

Voting for this year's midterm elections just concluded, but Republican officials in a number of states are already looking to shape how votes are cast in 2028.

Twelve GOP state attorneys general are pushing to revive the president's bid for mail-in voting restrictions in time for the 2028 election.

On Thursday, they started the process of appealing a September order by U.S. District Judge Carl Nichols, one of the two judges who blocked the U.S. Postal Service from carrying out a plan released in response to an executive order by President Trump.

The Republican state attorneys general represent Alabama, Florida, Indiana, Kansas, Louisiana, Missouri, Montana, Nebraska, Oklahoma, South Carolina, South Dakota and Texas. It's not clear, however, how long some of these states will continue this case, given that Democrats won up and down the ballot in the midterms. In Texas and Kansas, Democratic candidates are set to take control of their states' attorney general's offices in January.

In September, the Supreme Court refused to pause a similar ruling by U.S. District Judge Indira Talwani, who is based in Boston. That order stopped USPS from working on its revised rule for federal ballot mail, but it only applied to this year's midterm elections.

Nichols' preliminary injunction blocks USPS from implementing the plan for all federal elections, including the 2028 race.

It's not clear if the Trump administration plans to appeal Nichols' ruling by Friday's deadline for filing a court notice. Asked about the Justice Department's plans, DOJ spokesperson Matthew Tragesser replied in an email that the department doesn't comment on ongoing litigation.

The blocked rule — which the Postal Service released in late August — would require states to turn over lists of voters' names and addresses in order to have them delivered by USPS.

Nichols, a Washington, D.C.-based judge who was nominated by Trump, found that the mailing agency likely has no power to impose that requirement on states.

"As the Government concedes, the Postal Service could issue (and enforce) the Rule only if Congress gave it the authority to do so, but here no statute grants the Postal Service the power to issue key parts of the Rule," Nichols wrote.

The administration's earlier push to put these new restrictions in place for the midterms alarmed many election officials, who were concerned about last-minute changes causing major disruptions to the tens of millions who regularly vote by mail. Some voters with disabilities and those in places without polling sites, they feared, could have lost the ability to exercise their right to cast a ballot.

A whistleblower report claimed the online system officials would need to use to follow USPS' revised ballot requirements had not been properly tested and could have resulted in many eligible voters not getting their mail-in ballots in time or at all.

While the Supreme Court ultimately stopped implementation of the USPS rule for the midterms, Justices Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas dissented from that ruling.

Fellow conservative Justice Brett Kavanaugh said in a concurring opinion that he believed state and local election officials did not have enough time to "reasonably implement the rule" this time. But Kavanaugh noted that "there is at least a fair prospect that the final rule falls within the Postal Service's statutory authority."

Edited by Benjamin Swasey

entries.title: FAA issues nationwide ground stop for all U.S. airports
entries.summary: The FAA has issued a nationwide ground stop for all U.S. airports following a "communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers," according to Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy.
entries.content:
FAA issues nationwide ground stop for all U.S. airports

The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has issued a rare nationwide ground stop for all U.S. airports following a "communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers," which is currently under investigation, according to Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy.

Friday afternoon, the FAA said in a post on X that there has been a "temporary telecommunications outage."

"Out of an abundance of caution all flights have been halted. Every flight has been accounted for and international flights will be handled on a case by case basis," the post reads.

The outage hasn't been linked to a threat or attack, said Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin.

"There is no indication, and we had no reason to believe as of right now that this was a threat to the United States," Mullin told reporters at the White House. "There's no reason for the public to be afraid or scared for your loved ones."

The U.S. last issued a ground stop of this scale in 2023, when all U.S. airports were shut down due to an outage in the NOTAM (Notice to Air Missions) system, which alerts pilots and airports of real-time hazards.

That outage prompted fears of a cyberattack, but the FAA later determined the issue was caused when contract workers inadvertently deleted critical files.

The telecommunication issue doesn't extend to the entire U.S., Mullin said. Without naming the regions in question, he stated, "there's two areas inside the United States that are still able to communicate just fine."

Mullin also said that other countries' aviation systems don't seem to be affected by the FAA outage.

The FAA has recently begun rolling out an AI-enhanced software tool known as the SMART system as part of its ambitious overhaul of the nation's air traffic control system. But Air Space Intelligence, the company that makes the tool, quickly dismissed speculation that its product could be connected to the flight disruptions.

"The current ground stop is not based on or a result of the SMART system, any product of ASI or our integration with FAA and ATC," the company said on social media.

Passengers stranded

The nationwide ground stop has caused chaos in airports and headaches for travelers — many of whom are already too familiar with flight delays and cancelations during the holiday season.

At Dallas Fort Worth International Airport, Regina Harling said she waited hours — long past when her flight was supposed to depart — before she learned of the nationwide grounding by checking the news on her phone.

"There's still a sign right in front of me that says we're boarding in 16 minutes," she said.

Harling needed to travel last minute to San Diego for a family emergency. Stuck at the airport, she's thinking about how soon she can make it to her family, but she's not optimistic.

"I was just thinking to myself that it always feels like it's getting harder to travel than it used to be," she said.

This is a developing story.

Deepa Shivaram contributed to this report.

entries.title: What's Trump's strategy now with Iran? To keep things as they are
entries.summary: President Trump says the "status quo" is what Gulf Arab allies want as the Iran war hits a stalemate and the U.S. midterms force a pivot from threats of attacks to economic pressure.
entries.content:
DUBAI, United Arab Emirates — President Trump is confronting new realities nine months into the war with Iran that leave him with dwindling options to ending the conflict.

On Thursday, he waved away the need for a deal with Iran, saying the U.S. has billions of Iran's dollars frozen in overseas accounts.

"We don't need a deal with Iran. Those days have long since passed. We've got their money," he wrote in a Truth Social post.

Negotiations with Iran are stuck with mediator Qatar working to bridge the divide. Trump met Qatar's prime minister at the White House this week, and said afterward that Gulf Arab allies prefer "the status quo" of continued economic pressure on Iran. He wrote that while the U.S. remains "locked and loaded," an attack at this point "seems to be quite unlikely."

That's a pivot from his threats to carry out quick, intense strikes on Iran in the days before he had to contend with two election setbacks.

Trump's wartime ally, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, whom he'd thrown his support behind, is on the cusp of being ousted from power after elections there.

Meanwhile, at home, Trump's party lost its majority in Congress in midterm elections. Vice President Vance blamed Republican losses on the unpopular war with Iran and the nature of U.S. relations with Israel.

With less room to room maneuver and Iran still defiant, Trump's strategy appears to be to keep things as they are, for now. That means the possibility of escalation still looms.

Senior UAE diplomat, Anwar Gargash, told an audience in the country's capital of Abu Dhabi this week that the region must "prepare for a prolonged period of uncertainty, in which neither a decisive resolution nor a stable regional order can be taken for granted."

Here's what keeping the status quo looks like.

Iran's chokehold on the Strait of Hormuz persists

Official Iranian social media accounts frequently post videos of attacks on ships in the Strait of Hormuz for violating Iran's new rules requiring permission to navigate the waterway, which was open and free to ships before the war.

The U.S., meanwhile, is assisting oil tankers through the Strait of Hormuz using a route that's close to Oman's coastline. While this has helped Arab states export their oil, it does not solve the bigger problem of how to bring back the pre-war production levels of other vital products like liquified natural gas, fertilizer and aluminum. Nor does a status quo allow countries like Kuwait, Qatar and Bahrain to import goods to their ports.

The International Monetary Fund says Gulf Arab states are in economic recession as a result of the war, despite higher oil prices. It says Kuwait, Qatar and Iraq's economies are contracting approximately 16% this year. Bahrain's is down 11%.

More limited strikes that could rapidly escalate

The U.S. is sending a third aircraft carrier with thousands of troops to the region, leaving open the possibility of another planned military escalation.

This week, Iran unveiled what it says is a new underground missile production site.

The U.S. and Iran are also still occasionally carrying out tit-for-tat for strikes.

On Friday, Iranian media said the U.S. struck one of its islands in the Strait of Hormuz. It's an area where Iran has radars and drone launch sites. Iran's Revolutionary Guard said it hit back, targeting an early warning U.S. radar in Bahrain.

Iran remains economically battered, starved of oil revenue

Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters this week there's no need for military action against Iran at this stage because economic sanctions are doing the job.

"The pain that they're feeling is, eventually you have to eat. Eventually you have to be able to pay your own fighters and your own security forces," Rubio said.

There's also a U.S. naval blockade at sea barring Iranian ships from transporting oil to countries like China. This blockade, according to the U.S. military, has cut Iran off from at least $25 billion in revenue so far.

One of the biggest economic blows, though, has come from the United Arab Emirates. The UAE announced over the summer it was severing all economic and trade ties with Iran. The UAE had been among Iran's biggest trade partners and local bank accounts were allegedly used by Iran's supreme leader and Revolutionary Guard to move money around.

Meanwhile, the U.S. military's Central Command announced a new operation, dubbed "Iron Gate," with other U.S. government agencies, aimed at preventing Iran from using land routes to transport advanced weapons across its borders and the Caspian Sea.

War in Yemen intensifies, draws in more countries

Another consequence of the conflict with Iran is the resumption of all-out war between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis in Yemen.

The Houthis, who are not a direct proxy of Iran but are supported by it, say Saudi airstrikes across Yemen have killed scores of people in past months, including nearly 60 this past weekend, many of them women and children in a village near the capital Sana'a.

Saudi Arabia, meanwhile, faces daily missile and drone attacks by Houthis, including some this week that hit its key East-West pipeline carrying crude oil to bypass the Strait of Hormuz. Another Houthi attack hit Saudi oil company Aramco's skyscraper headquarters in Riyadh's financial district.

Deadly Houthi attacks on Saudi airports have led to flights and high-profile events being canceled.

As the Yemen war drags on, Pakistan, Turkey and Egypt are among the countries entering the fray with defensive support to Saudi Arabia. The U.S. is assisting with intelligence on the Houthis.

The United Nations says some 330,000 Yemenis have been displaced by the renewed fighting between the Houthis and the Saudi-backed Yemeni government, exacerbating an already dire humanitarian crisis.

Efforts by mediators continue, neither side budges

Iran says it's prepared for a short-term pause on attacks on ships in the Strait of Hormuz, but insists that seven demands be met before entering into direct talks over its nuclear program.

"The message has been only one thing. These seven items are on the table. Take it or leave it," Hamidreza Gholamzade, Tehran municipality spokesperson, told NPR.

These demands include lifting sanctions, ending the naval blockade, unfreezing Iran's dollars in overseas accounts and enforcing a ceasefire across all fronts, which includes halting Israeli attacks in Lebanon and Gaza.

Rubio has described the conditions as "absurd."

There's also discussion on diluting and moving Iran's enriched uranium abroad. However, the head of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, Mohsen Rezaei, told Iran's state broadcaster Wednesday: "We will not remove even a shred of enriched nuclear material from Iran."

It's another indication of the gridlock.

NPR's Hadeel Al-Shalchi in Antalya, Turkey, and Ahmed Abu Hamada in Cairo contributed reporting.

entries.title: The Trump administration's voter roll crusade could continue
entries.summary: Election officials are preparing for the Trump administration's pressure tactics over potential noncitizens on state voter rolls to continue, though recent court rulings pose new obstacles.
entries.content:
The Trump administration's voter roll crusade could continue

In the weeks before Election Day, the Trump administration escalated its hunt for voter fraud and its pressure on election officials — especially in California — to crack down on illegal voting by non-U.S. citizens.

Now, with Election Day come and gone, election officials and civil rights attorneys are preparing for the administration to continue its search for noncitizens on state voter rolls, as well as what they see as intimidation tactics toward election officials.

"It's clear that there is this drive to try to conjure up facts that just don't exist. I don't think that's going to change," James Williams, county executive for California's Santa Clara County, told NPR. "So we fully are prepared to continue to deal with this."

In recent weeks, federal prosecutors announced criminal charges against dozens of people who are accused of voting or registering to vote without being a citizen. Yet compared to overall numbers of voters, noncitizen voting is exceptionally rare. And since summer, the administration has touted what turned out to be grossly inflated numbers of noncitizens on state voter rolls.

In mid-October, federal officials alleged they had found 20,000 "likely" noncitizens on California's voter rolls. The Department of Justice sued the state to try to force election officials not to count ballots of voters whose citizenship had not been verified. A federal judge and a federal appeals court rejected the DOJ's requests, and the U.S. Supreme Court declined to intervene.

In the days leading up to Election Day, with the lawsuit pending, U.S. attorneys in California sent grand jury subpoenas to several counties, asking for records related to how local officials responded to DOJ's demands.

Though DOJ dropped its lawsuit last week, it has not rescinded these subpoenas.

"We have ongoing cases and investigations in various states surrounding voter process," U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche said at a Thursday press conference. "We are actively, and will continue to investigate election integrity cases criminally and civilly, and that wasn't expected to start or stop — no matter what the results of the election were last week."

But recent unfavorable rulings for the Trump administration have created new obstacles for future federal attempts to intervene on state voter list maintenance.

"Do I think they will still keep at this? I do, but there are just a lot of court losses that are going to be really difficult for them to maneuver around," Anna Baldwin, director of voting rights litigation at Campaign Legal Center, told NPR. "They've hit substantial roadblocks because it's a lawless program that Congress has never authorized."

Recent court orders reaffirmed that states have the authority to run their elections and called into question the credibility of the federal government's data on noncitizens.

One key ruling, which came down the night before Election Day, found that DOJ and the Department of Homeland Security lack any statutory authority to distribute lists of purported noncitizens to election officials. In that order, a federal judge in Washington, D.C., wrote that taking that action also violates the Privacy Act. The federal government could appeal.

In an earlier order in October, a different D.C.-based judge vacated the DOJ's project of requesting unredacted voter rolls from states, seeking to compare that voter data to federal databases, and instructing states to remove suspected noncitizens. The ruling found those actions were unlawful and disenfranchised eligible voters. The DOJ has appealed.

The Department of Justice declined to comment on litigation or future plans, but said in a statement, "The Department will continue to enforce federal election laws and will evaluate matters based on the facts and the law."

Looming criminal proceedings and subpoenas to election officials

Federal prosecutors have vowed to continue tracking down noncitizen voting cases, as have some local prosecutors. San Luis Obispo District Attorney Dan Dow is investigating the potential noncitizen voters federal officials flagged in his county. He has so far charged one individual.

"It has always been a crime but I've never had a noncitizen case referred to me. When we got 63 of them, we said, 'We will look at them,'" Dow told NPR. "It is our duty to uphold California law."

Loyola Law School professor Justin Levitt, who was a White House adviser on voting rights in the Biden administration, said he expects "a trickle of actual follow-through on actual cases" of noncitizens voting. "And that is also entirely consistent with everything we knew for decades — which is that this does happen, but it doesn't happen very often."

What remains to be seen is whether the Justice Department will retreat from the criminal threats federal officials have waged against local election officials, or try to escalate those further.

In letters delivered to every California county in October, DOJ officials warned: "If persons knowingly tabulate ballots cast by individuals identified by federal agencies as noncitizens, they risk becoming aiders and abettors to a federal crime."

President Trump added on Truth Social: "They will all go to jail for a long period of time!!!"

In the days before Election Day, officials in Los Angeles County as well as Bay Area counties, including Santa Clara and Sonoma, received subpoenas from their local U.S. attorney's office to turn over records this month.

In Sonoma, the subpoena is for records about an individual the DOJ alleges may have voted in a past election without being a U.S. citizen, as well as records about how county officials responded to DOJ requests to segregate ballots of people on its list of possible noncitizens, according to Sonoma County Counsel Joshua Myers.

The Oct. 21 subpoena sent to Los Angeles County, which was reviewed by NPR, requests records related to how the registrar-recorder's office screens for unlawful voting by noncitizens, as well as records responding to federal correspondence, including the demand to segregate ballots.

The DOJ said it does not comment on alleged subpoenas. But the substance of the subpoenas has raised questions about whether there may be a criminal probe targeted at counties.

Williams of Santa Clara County declined to speak about the subpoenas but said criminal threats against government employees who are trying to lawfully administer elections "strikes at the heart of what it means to live in a free society."

Looking forward, Williams said he is hoping for a way to productively collaborate with the federal government again.

"We should be aligned — federal, state and local government — in facilitating every citizen exercising their right to vote. And of course, we want voter rolls that don't include noncitizens," he said. "There's no disagreement about that."

Inflated and inaccurate lists

Another hurdle for the federal government's efforts to publicize purported noncitizens on voter rolls is the inaccuracies in its tallies so far.

Trump claimed in July there were 250,000 noncitizens registered in four states, including in California. But state officials pushed back on the data, and federal officials admitted the earlier numbers were a "ceiling" of potential noncitizens. In mid-October, federal officials had sent California its list of 20,000 "likely" noncitizens registered to vote in the state.

The federal government has never maintained a complete list of U.S. citizens. Trump administration efforts to cobble together citizenship data from various sources have led to naturalized citizens being mistakenly flagged as noncitizens, and data experts have warned the federal government's methodology in California was likely to also lead to false matches.

The weekend before Election Day, a federal judge allowed data experts from University of California Los Angeles' Voting Rights Project to analyze the DOJ's list of 20,000 names. The analysis found 42% did not appear on California's current voter roll and that naturalized citizens were on the list.

Separately, several California counties have noted the lists from DOJ were riddled with duplicates and obvious inaccuracies.

Santa Cruz County's top election official, Tricia Webber, wrote in an email that of the 81 people DOJ had listed as suspected noncitizens registered to vote in her county, "more than half are not registered in Santa Cruz County; some names do not match any person currently registered or previously registered," and some dates of birth "were wildly inaccurate with some dates appearing well into the future like 2044."

Even DOJ attorneys acknowledged in court hearings under questioning from judges that there have been flaws with federal lists of likely noncitizens.

U.S. District Judge David Carter, a Clinton nominee, who was presiding over the federal government's lawsuit against California, had planned to hold proceedings that would assess the accuracy of DOJ's lists. That will no longer happen since the DOJ dropped its lawsuit.

For Loyola Law School's Levitt, questions remain about whether federal officials violated the Privacy Act by using California voter roll data for this project without following required public notice procedures.

And with Democrats winning control of Congress, lawmakers could hold hearings that probe deeper into how federal officials came up with their list, said David Becker, the executive director for the Center for Election Innovation and Research.

"I think we're going to have some very serious scrutiny of the Department of Homeland Security and their methodology as they assisted the administration in its failed effort to try to demonstrate there was widespread noncitizen voting in this country," Becker said.

entries.title: Does Europe regret its bet on U.S. defense?
entries.summary: Europe bet big on American defense technology and they're now paying the price. Years-long backlogs are underway due to production delays and the U.S. own military needs.
entries.content:
Does Europe regret its bet on U.S. defense?

You're reading a newsletter from The Indicator from Planet Money. Once a week, we curate our favorite stories and insights on business, finance, economics and why they matter. Subscribe here to get it in your inbox every Friday.

Fox has officially acquired Roku and there are CONSEQUENCES. For one, the "Marine Aquarium" screensaver will no longer be available. One person posted on the "Mildly Infuriating" subreddit: "I can't believe it I love my fish what am I gunna do."

The artist behind that screensaver, Jim Sachs, is NOT renewing his license due to Fox's acquisition. "It seems that Fox simply wants another venue for spreading their philosophy, which I consider repugnant. I can't stand the idea of my artwork being used to lure even one person down that rabbit hole," Sachs told Ars Technica. The licensing deal will have big personal consequences for Sachs, who relies on the $80,000 per year licensing deal. Another comment on the subreddit posted, "This is the last straw, Apple TV for me."

Coming up

  • The U.S. can't keep up with defense demand
  • How housing affects fertility rates in Spain
  • What Walmart stock has to do with the economy

News We're Watching

Did Europe make a bad bet on American defense tech? - Bruegel

What to Know: Over the past decade, European countries have become increasingly reliant on U.S. technology to support their air defense systems. We're talking fighter jets & missile defense systems like the Patriot, which can intercept ballistic missiles. It seemed like an obvious choice: these are high-quality pieces of technology, they're readily available, and buying American keeps the U.S. committed to European defense. Here's the problem: the whole "readily available" thing doesn't seem to be true. There is a MAJOR backlog of missiles while demand just keeps going up. That's due to both production delays and the U.S.' own military needs in Iran. PLUS!! European countries that bought technology like the Patriot are now locked in to American equipment. They can't just switch to another supplier to get missiles.

Why this matters: You kind of want to know if you're not gonna get a few hundred missiles on time. While the U.S. is focused on the Iran war, threats from Russia still loom large in Europe. And now, many European nations are at the whim of these defense contracts panning out… having to put up with delays and higher costs. The article's authors look back and see a missed opportunity in 2022 for investment into homegrown systems: "Calls to Europeanise the funding and ordering of air defense systems were ignored and the strategic gap is now all too visible."

Business journalist and friend of the show Paddy Hirsch adds: "No one could have predicted the extent to which Trump would damage the relationship between the U.S. and Europe. But the fact is that Trump isn't the first president to beat the drum about European over-dependence on the US. He's just the first to really force the issue. And guess what? He was doing Europe a favor! Europe desperately needs to wean itself off the U.S. teat, and not just because of the unpredictability of a Presidential whim. But because there's no telling how U.S. and European interests will diverge over the next few decades."

Could more housing lead to a higher fertility rate? - Elcano Royal Institute

What to Know: Spain has one of the lowest fertility rates in the world. It's currently at 1.1, meaning 100 women birth 110 children on average. To maintain the current population, rates would need to sit at 2.1. Immigration has kept the population from dropping dramatically since 2000, but the author offers a DIFFERENT solution to Spain's childbearing woes: more housing. Spain, like many countries, has struggled with expensive housing: prices have risen 81% between 2015 to 2025. The average age of leaving the parental home in Spain is 30.2 compared to 23.8 in France and 24.1 in Germany. The author asks: could an influx of public housing incentivize partners to start families earlier?

How realistic is this?: There's no hard evidence in the Elcano article showing more housing actually leads to a higher fertility rate. That said, Planet Money co-host Jeff Guo says the evidence for this argument does look stronger outside the U.S. There was literally a paper about this topic IN SPAIN that came out a few weeks ago. The paper found a 10% rise in local housing prices LOWERS birth rates by about 3% for women 20-34. In fact, the authors deduced that higher housing prices account for roughly HALF of the 2014-2022 implied fertility rate decline. In short: more expensive housing = fewer kids.

Today's Indicator

The stock market might be the economy… just ask Walmart

If you HAVEN'T listened: We all know the old adage "the stock market doesn't equal the economy." Well, lately, maybe it does!! At least more than usual. The "new era" economy (AI, tech etc.) has an outsized impact on the growth of both the stock market AND economic growth. That's all well and good, except hyper-concentration means hyper-risk. If AI stocks start to tumble, it could have a negative chain reaction on the economy in a uniquely problematic way. Two non-profits in the episode warn that the AI bubble is a thing. In short, the economy depends on the market! A downturn there is more likely to mean an economic downturn too. Diversification is important, people.

If you HAVE listened: You know that the economic risk isn't just about a market downturn. It's about the impacts that follow. Consumer spending is driving much of economic growth, and that's led by wealthy spenders. Another downstream risk: pension funds hold debt related to the AI buildout, according to the report from the Open Markets Institute and Americans for Financial Reform Education Fund. They argue this has exposed pension funds and even ordinary workers to dangerous risk! Reporter Wailin Wong says, "That's something I wasn't able to get into in the episode, since we were focused on stocks and not debt. But certainly the credit markets are a huge part of this story too."

REST OF THE WEEK

  • The winners and losers of the Midterm Elections
  • Mike Schur and the Case of the Missing Sitcom
  • Why public schools are adding personal finance classes

In Our Spare Time

Reporter Ricky Mulvey read A Violent Masterpiece

It's a profane, no-holds-barred thriller. Jordan Harper wrote on TV shows in Hollywood before getting disillusioned with the industry and writing about some of its seedier parts in novels.

A Violent Masterpiece follows three storylines that converge around a suspicious death in a jail cell. It's Eyes Wide Shut meets LA Confidential.

Two things I really admire about Harper's work.

  • It's confidently modern. I think a lot of writers find more comfort writing about the distant past and allowing readers to find parallels to today. A Violent Masterpiece is confident and planted in the right now.
  • Harper's razor-sharp writing style. He cut his teeth writing for television, so his work is well-structured and every word counts.

A Violent Masterpiece is a perfect book to rip through on a plane if you are traveling for the holidays. A genteel reader should stay far away, and sickos should pick it up. The story is far from perfect; you'll see why at the ending. I loved it.

entries.title: How Sen. Chris Van Hollen plans to flex Democratic power on the foreign aid front
entries.summary: He's the ranking member of the Senate Foreign Relations Subcommittee that oversees health aid and he's just announced he's running for Majority Leader. He spoke to NPR about his foreign aid vision.
entries.content:
How Sen. Chris Van Hollen plans to flex Democratic power on the foreign aid front

"We need new leadership," says Senator Chris Van Hollen, who on Thursday announced he will challenge Chuck Schumer for Democratic majority leader. Van Hollen has garnered support among Democrats for his sharp criticism of the Trump administration, including their upheaval of U.S. programs to promote health and end poverty around the world.

In an interview with NPR on Tuesday, two days before his announcement, Van Hollen spoke to NPR about his plans to "shine a light on all the harm and damage the Trump administration's done to our country and our interests around the world" — and what the Democrats hope to accomplish with foreign aid.

As the ranking member of the Senate Foreign Relations Subcommittee, which oversees the State Department and what's left of the United States Agency for International Development, he could have considerable sway over how Congress investigates and legislates on foreign aid.

This interview has been edited for clarity and length. NPR reached out to the State Department for comment but did not receive a response in time for publication.

You've taken a strong stand against the Trump administration's shakeup of foreign aid. You led protests against the dissolution of USAID and in a hearing last year told Secretary of State Marco Rubio that "People died because of those actions, mothers, fathers and children." You've also authored statements condemning a range of actions, including tying health aid to mineral deals. In the majority, what's the first step you'd take on the aid front?

Priority number one is to do an analysis of all the harm the Trump administration has done.

There have been very credible analyses showing that over 700,000 people around the world died between January 2025 and January 2026 because of cuts to USAID. If these trends continue, you're talking about millions of people dying in the coming years.

One of the great benefits of being in the majority, is you actually have a gavel and can call a public hearing, and use that as a spotlight to help educate people around the country.

We can do that to show the consequences of Elon Musk taking a chainsaw to USAID. I remember to this day a scene at the White House [in February 2025] when Donald Trump was at his desk and Elon Musk was standing behind him, and a reporter asked Elon Musk about the cuts to fighting Ebola, and Elon Musk's response was essentially, "Whoops, yeah, we missed that." And then he claimed that they'd restored it. Well, we know that they've not restored it adequately — there's good evidence that the current Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo could have been better contained if the United States had not made big cuts to public health.

We can investigate what they did, not for the purpose of putting it back exactly as it was but understanding the damage that has been done, fully, with an eye toward reforming it.

You've already been speaking out against a lot of this in the minority. What kinds of actions can Democrats take as a majority that they couldn't before?

Being in the majority makes a big difference. Now we have many more tools available, specifically through the power of the purse.

One of the things the Trump administration has done is essentially sit on funds appropriated by the Congress for public health here at home but also for international health programs. So there's an example where we can much better safeguard the will of the Congress now that we're in the majority.

Can you give an example?

One of the things the Administration did was to rescind over $500 million in funds for global health. In other words, they cut it, and you had a rubber stamp majority in the Congress. Republicans, go along with that. You would never get Democrats to agree.

There's another ongoing example right now, which is a number of years ago, we passed about $1.5 billion in funds for [global] public health, and it appears that they're using those funds not for public health but to wind down USAID. So this is an area where we could say no, you may not use these funds to wind down USAID.

The administration has been ignoring a lot of these "no's" so far. What gives those "no's" more weight in the majority?

When we in Congress provide a sum of money, for say public health, we say this money should be spent on these specific items, like vaccinations or clinics. That's guidance, that's direction. It's technically called report language, and this report language used to be respected by Democratic and Republican presidents.

The Trump administration has ignored report language because it's not technically legally binding, and Republicans in the Congress have let them get away with it. And the more they let them get away with it, the more they do it.

So we're going to have to convert what used to be report language into real law to prevent this administration from taking those actions. We Democrats have been trying to do that, but since we've been in the minority, we haven't been able to get that passed.

What if the administration still tries to hold up funds or ignore or veto Congress' actions?

This has been a lawless president, and he's still in the White House. But being in the majority will give us more leverage. If we're able to codify the safeguards that would prevent the Trump administration from diverting funds from their intended purpose to something else, that would be legally binding. Then you can go to the courts and say, you know this isn't simply report language. This is not just guidance. This is legally required, and so that does provide the safeguards that we would need.

Now we may have a back and forth and fight with the administration over providing those safeguards, but we're in a much stronger position now than we have been.

If the Democrats win the presidency and keep control of Congress in 2028, would the fate of USAID be revisited? Might the agency return? Or are there parts of the Trump administration's global health policy that you think are worth preserving or building on?

I don't think there's anything the Trump administration has done that's worth preserving or building on. That does not mean that I'm in favor of simply returning to the status quo prior to this administration.

I am a big believer that the role that USAID performed was both helpful to protecting the health of Americans but also helpful to developing good relations with other countries and the people of other countries. I think we need to develop our plan for how we perform this very important role as part of our foreign policy and as part of our health policy. But I'm not saying we would just go back exactly to the way USAID was.

For stories about life in our changing world, subscribe to NPR's Global Health newsletter.

entries.title: Remembering singer and actor Peggy King
entries.summary: King, who died Oct. 25, got her start singing in big bands in the 1950s. She had a string of hits, a contract with MGM and was a popular fixture on TV variety shows. Originally broadcast in 1983.
entries.content:
Remembering singer and actor Peggy King

King, who died Oct. 25, got her start singing in big bands in the 1950s. She had a string of hits, a contract with MGM and was a popular fixture on TV variety shows. Originally broadcast in 1983.

DAVID BIANCULLI, HOST:

This is FRESH AIR. I'm David Bianculli. Today, Peggy King, a singer and actress who got her start singing in big bands in the 1950s and had a string of hits, a contract with MGM and was a popular fixture on many TV variety shows. She died late last month at the age of 96. Here she is in 1951, with Ralph Flanagan and his orchestra.

(SOUNDBITE OF SONG, "VERY GOOD ADVICE")

PEGGY KING: (Singing) I give myself very good advice, but I very seldom follow it. That explains the trouble that I'm always in. Be patient is very good advice, but the waiting tonight makes me curious. And I'd love the change should something strange begin.

BIANCULLI: Peggy King signed a long-term contract with Columbia Records and recorded two bestselling albums, "Wish Upon A Star" and "Girl Meets Boy." In 1952, MGM signed her to a movie contract. She was often told at MGM she looked and sounded like Judy Garland, something King disputed. She made a singing cameo in the film "The Bad And The Beautiful," and she became a regular on the TV variety shows, starring Mel Torme and George Gobel. She made guest appearances on other TV programs like "Dragnet." In 1955, on that show, she played a nightclub singer who may have encountered a suspect.

(SOUNDBITE OF TV SHOW, "DRAGNET")

KING: (As character, vocalizing).

(APPLAUSE)

UNIDENTIFIED ACTOR: (As character) That's sure a pretty song.

KING: (As character) Well, thank you very much. It's a new song written by a fellow named Arthur Hamilton.

UNIDENTIFIED ACTOR: (As character) Yeah, it's very nice.

KING: (As character) Now what's this about a man I'm supposed to have seen?

UNIDENTIFIED ACTOR: (As character) Well, we told you there was a shooting at 14th and Flower.

KING: (As character) Uh-huh.

UNIDENTIFIED ACTOR: (As character) Well, one of the people in the neighborhood recognized you, and he tells us that the suspect ran right by you, is that right?

KING: (As character) Gee, I don't remember. Just a minute. Oh, now I remember. Yeah. He ran out of the store, almost knocked me down, didn't even stop to say anything.

UNIDENTIFIED ACTOR: (As character) Did you get a good look at him?

KING: (As character) Well, he ran into me.

UNIDENTIFIED ACTOR: (As character) Can you tell us anything about him?

KING: (As character) Well, I'm afraid not. I didn't pay any attention. Something that happens and you don't think about it, you know?

UNIDENTIFIED ACTOR: (As character) Yes, ma'am. Would you know the man if you saw him again?

KING: (As character) I don't think so. The whole thing happened so fast.

UNIDENTIFIED ACTOR: (As character) There's nothing about him that you remember?

KING: (As character) No. Unless it was his eyes.

UNIDENTIFIED ACTOR: (As character) Ma'am?

KING: (As character) Well, his eyes, like he was looking right through you.

BIANCULLI: Peggy King also toured with the USO. Here she is with Bob Hope in 1956, performing for the troops during a stop in Alaska.

(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)

BOB HOPE: What are you going to sing for us?

KING: Well, Bob, I thought I'd do that terribly pretty member from "My Fair Lady," "I've Grown Accustomed To Her Face."

HOPE: Well, the stage is yours.

KING: Thank you. But I thought that since it's such a nice, intimate number, I wondered if I could go down there and sing it.

HOPE: Into the audience?

KING: Yeah.

HOPE: You mean down in that snake pit?

(APPLAUSE)

HOPE: She must be bucking for Section 8. Go, Peggy.

(LAUGHTER)

KING: (Singing) I've grown accustomed to your face.

BIANCULLI: Peggy King stopped performing in 1961 and moved to Philadelphia with her husband to raise their family. In the 1980s, after her children were grown, she returned to show business with renewed vigor. She sang with the Philly Pops Orchestra, the All-Star Jazz Trio and with other musicians. She performed in theaters and nightclubs and had stints in New York City at Michael's Pub and the Metropolitan Room. And she recorded new albums of standards, songs by Jerome Kern, Irving Berlin, the Gershwins and Rodgers and Hart. In tribute, we're going to listen to Peggy King's FRESH AIR concert from 1983. She was about to release her album "Rain Sometimes." At the piano was Michael Abene, who was featured on and wrote the arrangements for the album.

(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED NPR CONTENT)

TERRY GROSS: It's a great pleasure now to welcome and introduce singer Peggy King and pianist Michael Abene.

KING: Thank you.

(APPLAUSE)

KING: Thank you. Thank you, Terry, for not saying that you weren't born when I was singing before. I appreciate that very much.

MICHAEL ABENE: (Playing piano).

KING: (Singing) They all laughed at Christopher Columbus when he said the world was round. They all laughed when Edison recorded sound. They all laughed at Wilbur and his brother when they said that man could fly. They told Marconi wireless was a phony. It's the same old cry. They laughed at me wanting you, said I was reaching for the moon. But, ah, you came through. Now they'll have to change their tune. They all said we never could be happy. They laughed at us, and how. Ha-ha-ha, who's got the last left now? They all laughed at Rockefeller Center. Now they're fighting to get in. They all laughed at Whitney and his cotton gin. They all laughed at Fulton and his steamboat, Hershey and his chocolate bar. Ford and his Lizzie kept the laughters busy. That's how people are. They laughed at me wanting you, said it would be hello, goodbye. But, oh, you came through. Now they're eating humble pie. They all said we'd never get together. Darling, let's take a bow 'cause ha-ha-ha, who's got the last laugh? He-he-he, who's got the last laugh? Ha-ha-ha, who's got the last laugh now?

ABENE: (Playing piano).

(APPLAUSE)

KING: Thank you. That was from a film called "Shall We Dance." I think Fred Astaire sang that song. You'll find that I do a lot of songs that Fred Astaire sang. I love his singing. People look at me like I'm crazy, but I love his phrasing. I love what he does with the lyric. For a man with absolutely no voice, he's always been one of my favorite singers. And when I met him, I told him that, and he said - I said, oh, Mr. Astaire, I really love your singing. He said, you mean my dancing. And I said, no, I mean, your singing. And he said, God bless you, Peggy King. This is - I won't tell you the name. We'll just surprise you. This is a very - this is the oldest song we're doing. It's from 1928, and I absolutely love this song.

ABENE: (Playing piano).

KING: (Singing) I could cry salty tears. Where have I been all these years? Little wow, tell me now how long has this been going on? There were chills down my spine and some thrills I can't define. Listen, sweet, I repeat. How long has this been going on? Oh, I feel like I could melt. Into heaven I'm hurled. I know how Columbus felt finding another world. Kiss me twice, then once more. That makes thrice. Let's try for four-four. What a break for heaven's sake. How long has this been going on? Kiss me once, then once more. What a dunce I was before. What a break for heaven's sake. How long has this been going on? How long has this been going on?

(APPLAUSE)

BIANCULLI: That's Peggy King from a 1983 FRESH AIR concert. We'll hear more after a break. This is FRESH AIR.

This is FRESH AIR. Let's get back to our 1983 concert with Peggy King. She died late last month at the age of 96. She was a popular singer during the 1950s but stepped away from performing to raise a family. In the early 1980s, she returned to singing.

(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED NPR CONTENT)

KING: For those of you under 35, this song came from a film - a Gene Kelly film called "An American In Paris." For those of you a little older than that, it came from a 1938 movie by Sam Goldwyn called "Goldwyn Follies," I think.

(Singing) It's very clear, our love is here to stay, not for a year, but ever and a day. The radio and the movies and the movies that we know may just be passing fancies and in time may go. But, oh, my dear, our love is here to stay. Together we're going a long, long way. In time, the Rockies may crumble, Gibraltar may tumble. They're only made of clay. But our love is here to stay. But, oh, my dear, our love is here to stay. Together we're going a long, long way. In time, the Rockies may crumble, Gibraltar may tumble. They're only made of clay, but our love is here to stay.

(Singing) For you, for me, forevermore. It's bound to be forevermore. It's plain to see, we found by finding each other, the love we'd waited for. I'm yours. You're mine. And in our hearts, the happy ending starts. What a lovely world this world would be with a world of love in store for you, for me, forevermore. I'm yours. You're mine. And in our hearts, the happy ending starts. What a lovely world this world would be with a world of love in store for you, for me, forevermore.

(APPLAUSE)

KING: Thank you. That's - I didn't want to stop because I really wanted to go right into that. But that's from 1947 film. George Gershwin died in 1937. But when they started doing this, Ira rummaged around and came up with some wonderful old melodies, and he loved that one. And he put these words to it. It was from a Betty Grable film called "The Shocking Miss Pilgrim," which I saw. I was a little tiny girl, and I don't remember who the man was who sang it. Unless it was Dick Haymes. It was. Somebody here knows. OK, you're showing your age, sir.

(LAUGHTER)

KING: Thank you. Thank you. Those were all Ira and George Gershwin. And then, of course, you know that Ira went on to write with just about every one of the great composers, and he died just a few weeks ago. I thought it might be interesting to do some songs by a contemporary songwriter. And this is someone I know very, very, very well. When I was just coming away from Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer Films, where I had been sitting and filing my nails for several years and taking fencing lessons and things - all sorts of things like that and not doing much else, because it was the end of the big movie time. Arthur Freed had taken me there. I'd got a phone call. I did a local show, and I got a phone call from a young man named Arthur Hamilton, and he was working for Jack Webb on "Dragnet," and he said he'd written a song for me, and he'd like very much to have me come onto "Dragnet" and do it. And I did, and that began a very long and happy relationship. This first song by Arthur is the name of my new album, "Rain Sometimes." I don't think you've ever heard it. It was written in 1965, but it's a very nice song.

(Singing) Rain sometimes, money down the drain sometimes, reason to complain sometimes. That's how it'll be. But there'll be champagne sometimes, lobster flown from Maine sometimes. We'll ride the gravy train sometimes, just you wait and see. We may be stranded rain sometimes, dream our dreams in vain sometimes, lose more than we gain sometimes, but this I guarantee. Love is not for sometimes. Love is for all times, for all times, for you and me. Love is not for sometimes. Love is for all times, for all times, for you and me. Rain sometimes.

(APPLAUSE)

KING: It sounds like an old song, isn't it?

BIANCULLI: Peggy King performing in concert for FRESH AIR in 1983. She also spoke to Terry Gross about her life and music. She died late last month at age 96. After a break, we'll hear more from that FRESH AIR visit, and Justin Chang will review "Bitter Christmas," the new film by Spanish director Pedro Almodovar. I'm David Bianculli, and this is FRESH AIR.

(SOUNDBITE OF SONG, "LAZY AFTERNOON")

KING: (Singing) It's a lazy afternoon. And the beetle bugs are zooming, and the tulip trees are blooming. And there's not another human in view but us two.

BIANCULLI: This is FRESH AIR. I'm TV critic David Bianculli. Today, we're remembering Peggy King, the singer and actress whose career ranged from singing with big bands in the 1950s to recording best-selling albums and appearing as a regular on several TV variety shows. She died late last month at the age of 96. When she spoke with Terry Gross in 1983 as part of a FRESH AIR concert, she discussed her interpretations of some musical standards.

(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED NPR CONTENT)

KING: This next song will be very familiar to you because it's really become a classic. Before it had ever been recorded, before anybody ever did it, I opened up Mocambo at the height of "The Gobel Show." Hello, George. George is in Valley Forge today. Hello, George. And it was Arthur's birthday. And he had never heard this song done by anybody. It hadn't been recorded, and no one had done it anywhere. And he was sitting right there in the front row. And about halfway through the show, I said, Arthur, happy birthday.

(Singing) Now you say you love me. You cried the long night through. Well, you can cry me a river. Cry me a river. I cried a river over you. Now you say you're sorry for being so untrue. Well, you can cry me a river, cry me a river. I cried a river over you. You drove me - nearly drove me out of my head, while you never shed a tear. Remember, I remember all that you said. Told me love was too plebeian, told me you were through with me. And now you say you love me. Well, just to prove you do, come on and cry me a river. Cry me a river. I cried a river over you. You drove me, nearly drove me right out of my head, while you - you never shed a tear. Do I remember? Yeah, I remember all that you said. Told me love was too plebeian, told me you are through with me. And now you say you love me. Well, just to prove you do, come on and cry me a river. Cry me a river. I cried a river over you. I cried a river over you. I cried a river over you.

(APPLAUSE)

KING: Thank you. Thank you.

GROSS: Peggy, did you always plan on coming back to performing after you took your break?

KING: No. I really didn't plan to take that long a break. But I - you know, we moved to the suburbs. I had two children in a year and 10 days, and I was very busy. And, you know, I was - you know, the chauffeur. I was doing all the, you know, the PTA or whatever, those things. No, not the PTA, the Brownies. That's it. The Brownies. I was the greatest Brownie leader that you ever had. Right, Suzy? My daughter will tell you. But I never thought about it. I'm kind of a freak. If I don't sing for three or four years, then I open my mouth, and it's there. You know, one day, I'll open my mouth, and it'll be dust, you know, if I don't stop that. I think now that I'm older, I will have to warm up a little. My husband says that someone said to him, I'd like to use Peggy's warm-up thing, whatever she uses. And Sam said, that's easy. Peggy goes, (imitating clearing throat). That's live - that's because I did so much live radio and live television. You really didn't have a lot of time to get yourself together.

GROSS: You recorded several albums.

KING: Oh, yeah, I did a lot of albums with Columbia, yes.

GROSS: And you just went back into the studio and recorded one...

KING: Yes.

GROSS: ...That I think you produced yourself.

KING: I didn't produce it. Michael Abene produced it with the engineer, whose name is Jay Messina. They produced it.

GROSS: You had the kind of control, I think.

KING: I had a lot of input.

GROSS: What was the difference for you between what you wanted from the album now and what albums were like in the '50s?

KING: Well, the big difference was that Mitch Miller wasn't in the booth, and I - you know, I couldn't see all of that conducting. No. The major difference today in recording is that they do it in pieces. They do it in sections, you know, which we did not do the album in sections. We did it in three-hour sessions, right straight through. Michael felt very strongly, and so did I, that we would get more of an emotional recording if we did it all at once. I think you tend to lose some of the - when you've done a song over and over and over, it almost becomes too emotional for me. I get - you know, I never like singers who cry while they sing. I think the trick is to make everybody else feel like crying or laughing while you do not do it yourself. But if you sing a song like that over and over, you will cry just from sheer exhaustion. So I did - I don't think we did more than two takes on anything. We just kind of did it right through. And Michael plays so beautifully. I really didn't need to do that many takes.

GROSS: You have a lot more control that you did - than you did before, both in the recording studio, but also in terms of what you want to do. Like, you referred before to being at MGM, where it was in the tail end of the big studio days.

KING: Yes.

GROSS: And they created their performers into what their performers to be, and they told them what movies they were going to be in, and someone had very little control there. What kind of changes do you want to make in your career now? What kind of career do you want to have that's different from the one from the '50s?

KING: Well, I'm not one of those singers who ever says, oh, that song is - you know, that's a terrible song. For instance, one of the songs, the one I like almost the most on the album, is "I'm In Love Again," which is 1929 Gershwin, and, you know, everybody that I ever mentioned it to until Michael Abene said, oh, that's a corny song. It isn't. It comes out - it's terrific. I love it. I never turn a song down without looking at it. But I don't ever want to be told - I just don't want to be in one of those ruts again. I don't want to be told that I sound like Judy Garland or that I sound like - I don't know who else - Peggy Lee.

You know, I mean, by the time you finish your career, they'll tell you that you sound like everybody. You know, I don't really think that I sound like anyone. I don't copy anyone. I don't try to sing like anyone. And I think for the first time - you know, I'm a grown woman. I think people tend to take a grown person seriously. I'm not a kid. And I think that I want to be a little more relaxed. I was - I'm not hungry any longer. I don't have to make a living. That's a terrible thing to say, but you are - tend to be a little more relaxed when you know that an ax is not going to fall and tomorrow you're going to be on the street. You know, it is a little different.

BIANCULLI: Peggy King appearing in concert on FRESH AIR in 1983 and speaking with Terry Gross. More after a break. This is FRESH AIR.

(SOUNDBITE OF MUSIC)

BIANCULLI: This is FRESH AIR. We're devoting today's show to Peggy King, the singer and actress who died late last month. She was 96 years old. In 1983, when she performed in a FRESH AIR concert, she talked about some of her favorite songwriters.

(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED NPR CONTENT)

KING: My - if I had to choose a favorite set of - I love Jerome Kern, and I sing a lot of Kern. But I really, really love the lyrics of Lorenz Hart. I think there has never again been anyone of his like. He was the most prolific, the most incredible lyricist that ever lived. He was a dynamic little man - under five feet. He never ran - he never walked when he could run, they say, and he never he never giggled when he could laugh, and he never talked when he could scream. You know, he was - there were no grays, and I understand that because that's me. He was just all-out. And he had an unhappy life. He had an unhappy time.

The world wasn't really ready for his personal life. And he was in Philadelphia doing a show and kept running to Wanamakers and buying raincoats and overcoats because he kept running out without them, getting cold. And he did that once too often, and he died at a very, very young age. But he left us this incredible legacy.

Richard Rodgers, of course, went on to write with the great Oscar Hammerstein, and that's wonderful, too. But for me, there isn't anything like Rogers and Hart.

(Singing) Once I was young. Yesterday, perhaps. Danced with Jim and Paul and kissed some other chaps. Once I was young, but never was naive. I thought I had a trick or two of my imaginary sleeve. And now I know I was naive but I didn't know what time it was. Then I met you. Oh, what a lovely time it was. How sublime it was, too. I didn't know what day it was. You held my hand. Warm as the month of May, it was. And I'll say it was grand. Grand to be alive, to be young, to be mad, to be yours alone. Grand to see your face, feel your touch, hear your voice, say I'm all your own. But I didn't know what year it was. Life held no prize. I wanted love, and here it was, shining out of your eyes. I'm wise. And I know what time it is now. Grand to be alive, to be young, to be mad, to be yours alone. Grand to see your face, feel your touch, hear your voice, say I'm all your own. But I didn't know what year it was. Life held no prize. I wanted love, and here it was, shining out of your eyes. I'm wise, and I know what time it is now.

(APPLAUSE)

KING: Thank you. This is my favorite song of all. I think it's the unhappiest. It's from "Slaughter On Tenth Avenue," and I think it's the greatest verse ever written by anybody. You have to picture the girl singing this song looking in a mirror. It's very important.

(Singing) Look at yourself. If you had a sense of humor, you would laugh to beat the band. Look at yourself. Do you still believe the rumor that romance is simply grand? Since you took it right on the chin, you have lost that bright toothpaste grin. My mental state is all a jumble. I sit around and sadly mumble. Fools rush in. So here I am. Very glad to be unhappy. I can't win, but here I am, more than glad to be unhappy. Unrequited love's a bore. And I've got it pretty bad. But for someone you adore, it's a pleasure to be sad. Like a straying baby lamb with no mammy and no pappy I'm so unhappy. But oh so glad.

(APPLAUSE)

BIANCULLI: Peggy King appearing in concert and speaking to Terry Gross in 1983. She died October 25 at age 96. You can find her other appearances on FRESH AIR at freshairarchive.org. Let's conclude our tribute to Peggy King with this Jerome Kern song.

(SOUNDBITE OF SONG, "DEARLY BELOVED")

KING: (Singing) Dearly beloved, how clearly I see. Somewhere in heaven you were fashioned for me. Angel eyes knew you. Angel voices led me to you. Nothing could save me, fate gave me a sign. I know that I'll be yours come shower or shine. So I say merely, dearly beloved, be mine.

BIANCULLI: Coming up, Justin Chang reviews "Bitter Christmas," the newest film by Spanish director Pedro Almodovar. This is FRESH AIR.

entries.title: USMNT head coach Mauricio Pochettino is leaving for Manchester United
entries.summary: Mauricio Pochettino is out as head coach of the U.S. men's national soccer team. Pochettino led the U.S. to the round of 16 at last year's World Cup. He's departing to coach Manchester United.
entries.content:
USMNT head coach Mauricio Pochettino is leaving for Manchester United

Mauricio Pochettino, who took over an ailing U.S. men's national soccer team in 2024 and led the squad to a Round of 16 finish in the 2026 FIFA World Cup, is departing to take over as coach of the famed English Premier League club Manchester United.

Pochettino was the highest-profile manager the U.S. men's team had ever hired. His aggressive attacking style of play won praise from his players and fans alike. At the 2026 World Cup, the USMNT finished first in its group and won its first knockout-round game since 2002. Pochettino's three wins were the most at any World Cup by a USMNT coach.

In a press conference Friday, an emotional Pochettino described the move as "one of the most difficult decisions" of his career. He had been "excited" about the project of revamping the U.S. men's national team, he said, but ultimately the offer from Manchester United represented "the next step to try to make your dreams come true." 

U.S. Soccer CEO J.T. Batson credited Pochettino with raising the standard across the federation, and especially the men's program, which has long been viewed as a cut or two below traditional soccer powers in Europe and South America yet has ambitions of competing at the highest levels. "The belief of what's possible for soccer in this country has never been higher," Batson said.

When Pochettino arrived, there were only about 18 months remaining before last summer's World Cup. In that limited time, he set out to tear down what he saw as a culture of complacency and rebuild the roster from the ground up. He evaluated more than 70 players, ultimately uncovering several key contributors to the World Cup roster.

"He's meant so much to me. He's helped me develop as a player and as a person. As a player, that's all you can ask for, to have that trust and that belief in you," said midfielder Sebastian Berhalter.

As a player, Pochettino represented Argentina in the 2002 World Cup and played in soccer leagues in Spain and France. As a coach, he managed some of Europe's most recognizable clubs: Tottenham Hotspur, Chelsea and Paris Saint-Germain. In August, he signed an extension to lead the USMNT through the 2030 World Cup, giving him a full four-year cycle to build the team into a true contender.

Pochettino will lead the U.S. for two more games — both against Haiti in the coming days — before departing for Manchester United.

Steve Cherundolo, the former USMNT player and former head coach of the MLS club LAFC, will take over as interim head coach while U.S. Soccer searches for a permanent replacement for the next cycle leading up to the 2030 World Cup.

"Our ambition is high, and we believe that this is one of the great coaching jobs in the world," Batson said.
